title: Scotch whisky under pressure: costs, trade and where to grow next
label: 11 November 2026 · Scotland’s whisky industry: Tariffs, trade and growth
summary: The Committee heard that Scotch whisky faces a difficult global backdrop: uneven growth driven by high energy prices and an AI-related trade boom, persistent tariff risk and growing competition. Witnesses agreed the industry must diversify export markets, secure better implementation of trade deals (notably with India), and get clearer government support on export promotion, energy costs and tax. Smaller distilleries are especially vulnerable because of long production lead times, local infrastructure limits and rising business costs.

chapters.title: A hard global backdrop
chapters.takeaway: High energy prices, an uneven global boom in AI-related trade and geopolitical uncertainty are squeezing exporters like Scotch whisky.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To start, how do current UK and global economic conditions affect an export-led sector such as Scotch whisky?

turns.speaker: Will Haworth
turns.text: Exporters are hit by a patchwork of unilateral and transactional trade moves, plus conflicts pushing up energy and input costs. Scotch relies heavily on exports, so tariffs and hidden trade barriers hurt deeply and can have long-lasting effects.

turns.speaker: Dr Sampson
turns.text: Two big shocks matter now: high energy prices and a surge in trade for AI hardware. Countries supplying energy or AI hardware are doing well; energy importers like the UK are not. That squeezes demand for luxury exports.

turns.speaker: Professor Khorana
turns.text: World GDP is sluggish and inflation remains elevated. UK business investment is flat or falling. For Scotch—very exposed to global demand—slower growth, high transport and energy costs, and trade fragmentation all weigh on competitiveness.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are the top risks to watch next?

turns.speaker: Professor Khorana
turns.text: A big risk is falling business investment because firms' planning horizons are long. Also, sustained high energy costs (UK energy prices are much higher than many competitors) would hit an energy-intensive sector like whisky.

turns.speaker: Dr Sampson
turns.text: An escalation of conflicts—Ukraine/Russia or in the Middle East—or an end to the AI boom would dent global demand and therefore exports of Scotch.

turns.speaker: Will Haworth
turns.text: We should expect more policies that favour domestic manufacturing and shorten supply chains within geopolitical blocs, rather than global, frictionless trade. That shifts the baseline for exporters.

chapters.title: Tariffs, trade deals and market access
chapters.takeaway: Tariffs and trade policy uncertainty (especially US tariffs) make market diversification and careful implementation of FTAs critical for Scotch.

turns.speaker: John Cooper
turns.text: With demand shifting globally—India growing fast in volume—should Scotch firms invest more in marketing higher-value products in those markets?

turns.speaker: Professor Khorana
turns.text: Yes. India’s growth has been in lower-priced bulk and bottled blends. To get higher value you need targeted promotion and access to finance for firms to invest at the premium end.

turns.speaker: Will Haworth
turns.text: Diversification is vital. The UK has signed post‑Brexit FTAs—India, CPTPP membership, Gulf deals—but other players, notably the EU, are also pursuing deals. Scotch firms should push the UK to match competitors’ market access quickly.

turns.speaker: Dr Sampson
turns.text: An SPS arrangement with the EU likely won’t directly bite Scotch, but a customs union would. Re-entering an EU customs policy would force us to inherit EU external deals and give up independent ones; the net effect varies by market.

turns.speaker: Will Haworth
turns.text: The US experience is instructive: tariffs imposed in 2019, lifted, returned and lifted again. US trade policy looks structurally tougher; do not plan on easy, permanent access. Diversify where possible.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: What did the US tariffs teach exporters about uncertainty?

turns.speaker: Will Haworth
turns.text: They showed that politically driven tariffs can be volatile and are hard to predict. For Scotch, access to other markets and a strong export promotion effort are insurance against that volatility.

turns.speaker: Dr Sampson
turns.text: Tariffs coming from unrelated trade disputes often hit politically salient industries like Scotch as collateral damage. That’s a real ongoing risk—especially with UK-China and UK-US tensions.

chapters.title: Winners, losers and the long lead time
chapters.takeaway: The industry’s long production timelines make it especially vulnerable to shocks; smaller distilleries and those selling mainly in the UK are most exposed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How have trading conditions changed for producers, and are smaller distilleries worse off?

turns.speaker: Anthony Wills
turns.text: Single malt growth was strong until 2022. Since then demand has softened. Small distilleries can’t match big companies on price and are hit by transport and fuel surcharges—they’re more exposed when markets slow.

turns.speaker: Annabel Thomas
turns.text: We’ve had double-digit growth from a small base but it’s getting harder. Smaller producers rely on independent bars and retailers who themselves face cost pressures, so the distribution channel is under strain.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brenton
turns.text: Larger firms are also affected. Sales were down around 2% last year and the industry is below its peak. We’ve reduced some production but must plan for the long term because whisky is matured years before sale.

turns.speaker: John Cooper
turns.text: Does over‑production mean consolidation is coming?

turns.speaker: Anthony Wills
turns.text: Yes. Distillery numbers rose sharply since the 2000s. Many expanded assuming continued growth; the correction is already causing insolvencies and will force consolidation.

turns.speaker: Mr MacDonald
turns.text: Is the rise in bulk spirit exports—'bulk whisky'—damaging premium Scotch?

turns.speaker: Dr Sampson
turns.text: It’s a risk. The industry must protect the premium brand and keep consumer perceptions clear between bulk spirit and premium Scotch.

turns.speaker: Maureen Burke
turns.text: After tariffs are removed, how long until exports recover?

turns.speaker: Professor Khorana
turns.text: Recovery takes time; tariffs change market behaviour and consumer patterns. Expect medium- to long-term effects, not a quick bounce-back.

turns.speaker: Dr Sampson
turns.text: Expect sluggish responses because producers base investment on future tariff risk as well as present rates. Temporary tariff drops won’t automatically restore investment confidence.

chapters.title: Costs at home: tax, energy and infrastructure
chapters.takeaway: High UK excise duty, energy costs, and local infrastructure limits are major and immediate pressures; the industry wants targeted government support.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Why are UK energy prices so high and how does that affect whisky firms' decisions to adopt renewables?

turns.speaker: Professor Khorana
turns.text: I’m not an energy specialist, but grid constraints, ageing infrastructure and international shocks push UK prices up. Distilling and glassmaking are energy-intensive, so this hurts competitiveness.

turns.speaker: Kenneth Stevenson
turns.text: Why aren’t distilleries switching to on-site renewables or electric boilers?

turns.speaker: Annabel Thomas
turns.text: We use a lot of on-site renewables, but our site has a single-phase grid connection so we can’t export to the grid or scale solar efficiently. Grid constraints and connection cost are real blockers for many smaller sites.

turns.speaker: Anthony Wills
turns.text: We’ve installed solar on warehouses and are exploring wind, but on islands like Islay fuel transport, conservation studies for turbines and housing shortages complicate decisions and raise costs.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brenton
turns.text: We’ve invested in technologies like MVR to cut energy demand, but grid connections and industrial energy support schemes often exclude food and drink. That feels like a strategic oversight.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: On tax: UK duty on spirits is very high. What do you want the Government to do?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brenton
turns.text: We want Treasury to recognise dynamic tax effects: heavy tax can dampen demand and reduce receipts. We argue for treating alcohol units equally across categories and for the Treasury to consider the wider local economic impact.

turns.speaker: Annabel Thomas
turns.text: Duty rises hit small producers particularly hard because UK is often our biggest market and changing duty every year is an administrative burden for producers and small retailers.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Is small-producer relief the answer, as seen for beer?

turns.speaker: Anthony Wills
turns.text: If relief is considered, it should be fair across sizes and clear. Definitions of 'small' are tricky and you don’t want perverse incentives, but our concern is the overall level of duty and competitiveness.

chapters.title: Local communities, connectivity and practical barriers
chapters.takeaway: Distilleries are important local employers but face housing, transport and connectivity limits; better infrastructure and tailored support would preserve jobs.

turns.speaker: Susan Murray
turns.text: How are distilleries contributing to rural jobs, and what knocks to that local economy are you seeing?

turns.speaker: Annabel Thomas
turns.text: We set up to create local jobs on Morvern. National insurance rises reduced our affordable headcount. Housing shortages limit recruitment; community-led broadband helped operations but running it is a volunteer burden.

turns.speaker: Anthony Wills
turns.text: On Islay we had near-full employment. Redundancies and transport woes have reversed that growth. Distilleries provided housing solutions in the past; now infrastructure has not kept pace with expansion.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brenton
turns.text: Larger producers also prioritise local sourcing—barley mainly from Scotland—and keep buffers of stock in remote sites. But bottling and transport need reliable roads, ferries and energy.

turns.speaker: Susan Murray
turns.text: Has improved digital connectivity made a difference?

turns.speaker: Anthony Wills
turns.text: Yes—better broadband lets us barcode stock and work remotely. It helps tourism too, but ferry reliability remains a major constraint for islands.

chapters.title: What Government should prioritise
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses want the UK to secure and implement FTAs faster, improve export promotion with evaluation, include whisky in industrial strategy, and address energy and tax burdens.

turns.speaker: Dr Sampson
turns.text: Top priorities are market access (negotiate and implement FTAs), better export promotion with evaluation of what actually works, and market diversification to reduce exposure to shocks.

turns.speaker: Will Haworth
turns.text: The UK should match competitors’ offers in key FTAs, resource trade policy and export promotion properly, and help firms with export finance and trade facilitation.

turns.speaker: Professor Khorana
turns.text: Scotch could be more visible in the UK industrial strategy. The Government could use targeted export finance, energy support and active monitoring of FTA implementation, for example in India.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brenton
turns.text: We need recognition that excise, EPR costs and energy collectively harm the sector and communities. Specific asks: better access to industrial energy support and an evidence-based look at tax impacts on receipts and jobs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all—this session has highlighted the interplay of global trade risks, domestic costs and practical constraints for Scotch. We appreciate your time and evidence.
